title: First 16-Bit Wave & the 8-to-16 Bridge I: The TI TMS9900, TI-99/4A & TMS9995 (1976–1984)
summary: Part I of the 'First 16-Bit Wave & the 8-to-16 Bridge' Quest Arc: a relaxed, first-principles yet architecturally concrete 100-question journey through the Texas Instruments TMS9900, the TI-99/4 and TI-99/4A home computers, and the redeemed 40-pin TMS9995. Building smoothly on learners' 8-bit Intel-Zilog and Motorola-MOS foundations, this module traces how TI shrank a 16-bit minicomputer onto 64-pin silicon with RAM-resident registers, hardware multiply and divide, and bit-addressable serial I/O—and why console bus bottlenecks, double-interpreted BASIC, and cartridge gatekeeping obscured a remarkable architecture until the TMS9995 arrived.
topic_prompt: Part I of the 'First 16-Bit Wave & the 8-to-16 Bridge' Quest Arc (building on learners' 8-bit foundations from the Intel-Zilog and Motorola-MOS arcs): a relaxed, first-principles yet architecturally concrete 50-chunk journey through the Texas Instruments TMS9900 and its TMS9995 descendant (1976–1984). Explain every hardware and ISA idea intuitively for an educated generalist: (1) shrinking the TI 990 minicomputer onto one of the earliest single-chip 16-bit CPUs, and why separate address/data buses forced a bulky 64-pin DIP, three supply voltages, and a 4-phase clock; (2) the radical Memory-to-Memory architecture—keeping only PC, Status (ST), and the Workspace Pointer (WP) on silicon while storing registers R0–R15 in external RAM; (3) ultra-fast context switches via BLWP/RTWP (and why RAM-resident registers made sense in 1976 before fast CPUs hit the memory wall); (4) genuine hardware 16-by-16 multiply (MPY), 32-by-16 divide (DIV), and XOP traps; (5) bit-addressable CRU (Communications Register Unit) serial I/O (SBO, SBZ, TB, LDCR, STCR) vs. byte-wide ports; (6) the cautionary tale of the TI-99/4 and TI-99/4A—cancelling the 8-bit-bus TMS9985, squeezing the TMS9900 behind a wait-state-heavy 8-bit bus multiplexer with only 256 bytes of fast 16-bit scratchpad RAM, trapping 16 KB of user RAM behind the TMS9918A Video Display Processor, and double-interpreting TI BASIC atop GROM-based GPL bytecode (versus assembly programmers running workspaces in the 256-byte scratchpad); and (7) TI's cartridge gatekeeping, the 1983 price war exit, and the late redemption of the 40-pin TMS9995 (256 bytes of on-chip 16-bit RAM, prefetch, signed MPYS/DIVS, Tomy Tutor, and Geneve 9640).

sections.title: 1. Shrinking the TI 990: One of the First Single-Chip 16-Bit CPUs
sections.summary: Meet the 1976 Texas Instruments TMS9900, born from shrinking the board-level TI 990 minicomputer architecture onto a single NMOS chip while most personal computers were still 8-bit. Explore why keeping the 15-bit word address bus and 16-bit data bus completely separate forced a towering 64-pin DIP package, and unpack the electrical overhead of three power rails (+5 V, −5 V, and +12 V) plus an external four-phase clock.

chunks.title: A Three-Inch Slab from Dallas
chunks.content_markdown:
In June 1976, the microprocessor world belonged to sleek 40-pin, 8-bit chips like the Zilog Z80 and the Motorola 6800 family. Then Texas Instruments placed an unmistakable giant on engineers' workbenches: the **TMS9900**, a ceramic chip over three inches long bristling with 64 metal legs.

Why build something so huge? Unlike startup designs invented from scratch for small microcomputers, the TMS9900 was a single-chip shrink of TI's rack-mounted **TI 990 minicomputer** family. The larger TI 990/10 used circuit boards full of discrete logic chips, while the compact TI 990/4 dropped the TMS9900 onto one board and ran the exact same 16-bit machine code.

That made the TMS9900 one of the earliest commercial single-chip 16-bit CPUs, offering true binary compatibility with an industrial minicomputer. Yet its dramatic 64-pin bulk immediately raised a practical puzzle: why couldn't TI squeeze this 16-bit processor into the standard 40-pin package that everyone else used?

questions.prompt: What existing computer line served as the direct architectural blueprint for the Texas Instruments TMS9900?
choices: The Intel 8080 microcomputer family
The TI 990 minicomputer family
The Motorola 6800 industrial series
The Zilog Z80 business workstation line
questions.explanation: Texas Instruments designed the TMS9900 as a single-chip implementation of its rack-mounted TI 990 minicomputer architecture, maintaining binary compatibility with board-level models like the TI 990/10.

questions.prompt: How did the TI 990/4 differ from its larger sibling, the TI 990/10?
choices: It ran a trimmed 8-bit subset of TI 990 instructions
It stored its operating system on external cassette tape reels
It omitted binary compatibility with larger rack-mounted TI 990 code
It used a single TMS9900 chip instead of discrete boards
questions.explanation: Both systems executed the same 16-bit TI 990 instruction set, but the TI 990/4 replaced the 990/10's multi-board discrete logic CPU with the single-chip TMS9900.

chunks.title: Dedicated Lanes and Word-Aligned Streets
chunks.content_markdown:
The answer to the 64-pin mystery comes down to traffic flow. Some early chips saved pins by making the same wires carry memory addresses on one beat and data on the next—like a narrow one-lane bridge where cars take turns. TI rejected that delay and gave the TMS9900 a **non-multiplexed bus**, meaning address wires and data wires stayed permanently separate so memory transfers happened at full speed without extra external latch chips holding addresses between beats.

Moving a full 16-bit value at once claimed 16 dedicated data pins. To reach 64 kilobytes of memory, you might expect another 16 address pins, yet TI needed only 15. That trick relied on **word-aligned addressing**: every 16-bit word occupies two consecutive bytes starting at an even address, so 15 lines select $$2^{15} = 32{,}768$$ word slots covering all $$65{,}536$$ bytes.

Even with one pin saved, 15 address lines plus 16 data lines already consumed 31 pins—leaving far too little room inside a 40-pin shell.

questions.prompt: Why did Texas Instruments choose a non-multiplexed bus for the TMS9900?
choices: To keep address and data lines separate for direct, full-speed transfers
To shrink the chip into an inexpensive 24-pin plastic package
To let two different CPUs share the same external data pins
To force memory chips to transmit only four bits per cycle
questions.explanation: A non-multiplexed bus assigns permanent, separate pins to addresses and data, avoiding the turn-taking delays and external address-latch logic required by multiplexed buses.

questions.prompt: How could the TMS9900 reach 65,536 bytes of memory using only 15 address pins?
choices: By compressing every program instruction to half its normal length
By borrowing an extra address bit from the interrupt pins
By addressing 32,768 two-byte words starting on even boundaries
By splitting RAM into two isolated banks switched by hand
questions.explanation: With word-aligned addressing, each 15-bit address selects one of 32,768 16-bit (two-byte) words, spanning all 65,536 bytes without needing a sixteenth address pin.

chunks.title: Three Power Rails and a Four-Beat Metronome
chunks.content_markdown:
Dedicated buses were only half the story behind the TMS9900's bulky footprint. Once 31 pins went to addresses and data, TI still had to fit four interrupt-priority inputs, serial peripheral lines, bus-control signals, and demanding power and timing wires. All told, 64 pins made circuit boards wider, sockets pricier, and hobbyist builds far trickier than 40-pin rivals.

Electrical requirements compounded that cost. Built with an older mid-1970s silicon transistor process (enhancement-mode NMOS, like the 1974 Intel 8080), the TMS9900 required three separate steady power voltages—$$+5\,\text{V}$$, $$-5\,\text{V}$$, and $$+12\,\text{V}$$—rather than the single $$+5\,\text{V}$$ supply that made the Z80 and 6809 so effortless to wire.

Worst of all, it could not tick on a simple single-wire clock. It demanded an external **four-phase clock**, four tightly staggered, non-overlapping timing pulses ($$\phi_1$$ through $$\phi_4$$) produced by a dedicated companion clock chip to march data cleanly through the processor's internal circuits.

questions.prompt: How did the TMS9900's power-supply requirements compare to those of the Zilog Z80 and Motorola 6809?
choices: It ran on a single low-power voltage shared with CMOS memory
It required three separate power rails instead of a single 5-volt supply
It drew a single 12-volt supply regulated directly inside the CPU
It switched between two alternating power rails on each clock beat
questions.explanation: Like the earlier Intel 8080, the TMS9900 needed three separate voltages ($$+5\,\text{V}$$, $$-5\,\text{V}$$, and $$+12\,\text{V}$$), whereas the Z80 and 6809 ran cleanly from a single $$+5\,\text{V}$$ supply.

questions.prompt: What is a four-phase clock as required by the TMS9900?
choices: Four staggered, non-overlapping timing signals supplied by an external clock chip
Four independent crystal oscillators letting the CPU run four programs simultaneously
A software timer that slows the processor down during four memory wait cycles
A power-saving feature that shuts off one quarter of the chip at a time
questions.explanation: The TMS9900 relied on an external clock generator to deliver four non-overlapping pulse phases ($$\phi_1$$ through $$\phi_4$$) that sequenced internal logic steps across each cycle.

chunks.title: Byte Quirks and Upside-Down Bit Numbers
chunks.content_markdown:
Word-aligned addressing saved a pin, yet it introduced two famous quirks that surprised programmers arriving from 8-bit machines. First, what happens when a program wants to change just one 8-bit character in memory, even though the TMS9900 has no pin to select an odd byte? The chip must quietly perform a hidden read-before-write dance: it fetches the entire 16-bit word, swaps in the single updated byte inside the CPU, and writes the complete 16-bit word back out.

Second, TI inherited a numbering habit from big minicomputers and IBM mainframes. Most 8-bit programmers labeled the rightmost, smallest-value bit as bit 0 and the leftmost bit as bit 7. TI did the exact opposite on its 16-bit words: **bit 0** was the leftmost, highest-value bit ($$2^{15}$$), and **bit 15** was the rightmost ones place ($$2^0$$). Reading a TMS9900 manual upside-down was a rite of passage for newcomers.

questions.prompt: Because the TMS9900 lacks a pin to address individual bytes directly, how does it write a single 8-bit byte to memory?
choices: It shifts the single byte out serially across the four-phase clock pins
It disables half of the external RAM chips during odd byte writes
It forces programmers to store every text character as a 16-bit word
It fetches the full word, updates one byte, and writes it back
questions.explanation: Lacking a lowest-bit byte-select pin on its word-aligned bus, the TMS9900 performs a read-modify-write sequence on the full 16-bit word whenever updating a single byte.

questions.prompt: In Texas Instruments' TMS9900 documentation, which bit of a 16-bit word is labeled bit 0?
choices: The extra carry flag bit appended to every bus transfer
The rightmost bit representing the smallest place value of one
The leftmost bit representing the largest place value of 32,768
The middle divider bit separating the upper and lower bytes
questions.explanation: Following minicomputer and mainframe convention, TI numbered bits from left to right, making bit 0 the most-significant bit and bit 15 the least-significant bit.

chunks.title: Big Ambition, Tight Silicon
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and admire what Texas Instruments pulled off in 1976. Despite a giant 64-pin ceramic package, triple power supplies, and a fussy four-phase clock, the TMS9900 delivered genuine 16-bit minicomputer computing on a single piece of silicon—moving full 16-bit words across a clean, non-multiplexed bus while keeping software compatible with larger TI 990 systems.

Yet shrinking a minicomputer onto a mid-1970s microchip created an acute real-estate crisis inside the silicon die itself. Manufacturing yields—the share of working chips salvaged from each silicon wafer—dropped fast whenever a chip grew too wide, leaving TI's engineers with a harsh transistor budget. Building a full 16-bit arithmetic unit and decoding minicomputer instructions ate up most of the available room.

There was simply no space left on silicon for sixteen big 16-bit general-purpose registers. Instead of cutting the architecture down to one or two tiny accumulators, TI made the most daring bet of its era: if registers won't fit inside the CPU, where else could they live?

questions.prompt: What major manufacturing constraint forced TI engineers to rethink where the TMS9900 kept its 16-bit registers?
choices: Fitting sixteen 16-bit registers on 1976 silicon would blow past the practical die-size budget
Federal minicomputer regulations barred single chips from holding more than three registers
The 64-pin ceramic package lacked enough electrical ground pins to power internal registers
Four-phase clocks could only synchronize arithmetic units and could not drive register storage
questions.explanation: On 1976 NMOS silicon, large dies suffered poor manufacturing yields, so building a full 16-bit datapath left too little silicon area for sixteen on-chip 16-bit registers.

questions.prompt: Which trade-off best summarizes the physical design of the original 1976 TMS9900?
choices: Minimal pin count and battery friendliness at the cost of 4-bit internal math
Strict 8-bit Z80 compatibility at the cost of dropping 16-bit data transfers
Built-in video graphics and sound at the cost of eliminating external memory
Full 16-bit minicomputer bus width at the cost of bulky support hardware
questions.explanation: The TMS9900 delivered a genuine non-multiplexed 16-bit minicomputer bus on one chip, but paid for it with a 64-pin DIP, three supply voltages, and an external four-phase clock.

sections.title: 2. The Memory-to-Memory Gamble: Three Silicon Registers & RAM Workspaces
sections.summary: Discover the TMS9900's boldest architectural break from both the Z80 and 6809: keeping only the Program Counter (PC), Status Register (ST), and Workspace Pointer (WP) on silicon while storing all sixteen general-purpose registers (R0–R15) in a relocatable 32-byte block of external RAM. See how pointing WP anywhere in memory freed scarce 1976 transistor space for a clean, orthogonal 16-bit instruction set.

chunks.title: Taking the Direct Page to Its Extreme
chunks.content_markdown:
If you have explored the Zilog Z80 and the Motorola 6809, you already know how creative 1970s designers got with register space. Zilog squeezed an extra shadow register bank onto the Z80 die so programs could flip between two register sets. Motorola gave the 6809 a relocatable Direct Page register that turned a chosen 256-byte strip of RAM into quick-access scratch memory.

Texas Instruments faced the same tight transistor budget on an even wider 16-bit processor. Putting sixteen 16-bit general-purpose registers directly on the TMS9900 die would require 256 microscopic storage latches plus dense selection wiring—crowding out everything else.

So TI asked an audacious question: why keep *any* general-purpose registers on silicon at all? If external RAM already holds thousands of bytes right outside the chip's pins, why not leave the entire register set sitting out in main memory?

questions.prompt: How many individual bit-storage latches would sixteen 16-bit on-chip registers have demanded on the TMS9900 die?
choices: 64 bit latches
128 bit latches
256 bit latches
512 bit latches
questions.explanation: Sixteen registers holding 16 bits each equals $$16 \times 16 = 256$$ bit latches, plus supporting selector circuitry—a steep silicon cost in 1976.

questions.prompt: Which earlier 8-bit idea most closely foreshadowed TI's decision to treat a relocatable slice of RAM like processor registers?
choices: The Motorola 6809's relocatable Direct Page register
The Zilog Z80's built-in dynamic RAM refresh counter
The Intel 8080's fixed hardware stack inside ROM
The Hitachi 6309's hidden CMOS power-down sleep mode
questions.explanation: Just as the 6809's Direct Page register let a movable slice of RAM act like fast scratch space, TI pushed the concept further by placing all sixteen general-purpose registers in relocatable RAM.

chunks.title: A Bookmark Instead of Sixteen Notebooks
chunks.content_markdown:
That bold leap produced TI's **memory-to-memory architecture**, a processor design where data operations read operands from memory and write results straight back to memory rather than hoarding them inside on-chip registers.

Inside the TMS9900 silicon sit just three user-visible 16-bit registers: the **Program Counter (`PC`)**, which tracks the next instruction; the **Status Register (`ST`)**, which holds comparison flags, math carry/overflow bits, and an interrupt mask controlling which priority levels can interrupt the CPU; and the star of the show, the **Workspace Pointer (`WP`)**.

Picture an accountant who refuses to haul sixteen bulky ledgers everywhere. Instead, she carries one metal bookmark (`WP`) and clips it onto the top of any 32-byte drawer in a filing cabinet. That 32-byte block of external RAM—sixteen consecutive 16-bit words—becomes the CPU's active **register workspace**, serving as general-purpose registers `R0` through `R15`. Move the bookmark, and an entirely different block of RAM instantly becomes `R0` through `R15`.

questions.prompt: Which three user-visible 16-bit registers actually live on the TMS9900 silicon die?
choices: Accumulator A, Index Register X, and Stack Pointer SP
Registers R0, R1, and the Status Register ST
Base Pointer BP, Segment Register CS, and Program Counter PC
Program Counter PC, Status Register ST, and Workspace Pointer WP
questions.explanation: The TMS9900 keeps only PC, ST, and WP on silicon; all sixteen general-purpose registers (R0–R15) reside in external RAM starting at the address stored in WP.

questions.prompt: How many bytes of external RAM make up one complete TMS9900 register workspace?
choices: 16 bytes, holding sixteen 8-bit registers
32 bytes, holding sixteen 16-bit registers
64 bytes, holding thirty-two 16-bit registers
256 bytes, matching a standard memory page
questions.explanation: A register workspace holds sixteen registers (R0 through R15) of 16 bits (2 bytes) each, totaling exactly 32 consecutive bytes of RAM.

chunks.title: Finding R4 Inside RAM
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's trace how the TMS9900 turns a register name into a real memory address. In TI assembly manuals, hexadecimal (base-16) numbers start with a `>` sign, so `>0100` means decimal 256. Suppose `WP` currently holds `>0100`, placing the active register workspace at byte 256 in RAM.

Because each register is two bytes wide, register `Rn` always sits at the simple formula $$\text{WP} + 2n$$. That puts `R0` at `>0100`, `R1` at `>0102`, `R4` at `>0108`, and `R15` at `>011E` (where hex `1E` equals decimal 30).

Now watch the instruction `A R1, R4` ('add `R1` to `R4`'). The CPU multiplies 1 by 2, adds `>0100`, and fetches the 16-bit word at `>0102`. Next, it computes `>0100 + 8`, fetches the word at `>0108`, sums both values in its 16-bit ALU, and writes the new total straight back to `>0108`—all without a single on-chip data register.

questions.prompt: If the Workspace Pointer (WP) holds decimal address 256, at which byte address does register R4 reside?
choices: Address 260, because each register occupies one byte
Address 262, because R0 is skipped for system flags
Address 264, because each 16-bit register spans two bytes
Address 272, because each register reserves four bytes
questions.explanation: Each register sits at $$\text{WP} + 2n$$. For $$\text{WP} = 256$$ and $$n = 4$$, R4 lives at $$256 + 2(4) = 264$$.

questions.prompt: When the TMS9900 executes the instruction A R1, R4, where does the final sum get written?
choices: Into an internal 16-bit accumulator hidden beside the ALU
Into the fixed stack area at the top of main memory
Into the Workspace Pointer register to advance the frame
Into the external RAM word located at WP plus eight bytes
questions.explanation: Because R4 lives in external RAM at $$\text{WP} + 8$$, the memory-to-memory add instruction writes the updated 16-bit sum directly back to that RAM address.

chunks.title: Symmetry, One Quirky Register, and Overlapping Desks
chunks.content_markdown:
Because registers *were* ordinary RAM words, TI's instruction set achieved remarkable regularity—what architects call an **orthogonal** design, where operations work uniformly across addressing modes. The exact same `A` (add) instruction could add a register to a register, a memory variable to a register, or even one memory location directly to another, using modes like indirect addressing and auto-increment (automatically advancing a pointer register after reading it).

Still, two clever twists kept programmers alert. First, `R0` could never serve as an index register when adding an offset to a base address: TI reused register code zero inside the instruction bits to mean 'no index register—use a plain direct address instead.'

Second, nothing stopped two register workspaces from *overlapping* in RAM! By placing a helper routine's `WP` just sixteen bytes past the caller's `WP`, the caller's `R8`–`R15` seamlessly became the helper's `R0`–`R7`—passing parameters instantly without copying a single byte.

questions.prompt: Why could TMS9900 programmers not use register R0 as an index register?
choices: Encoding zero in the index field signaled plain direct addressing instead
Register R0 was physically hardwired to store the constant value zero
Register R0 lived inside read-only memory and could never be changed
Indexing with R0 was reserved exclusively for hardware interrupt priority lookups
questions.explanation: In the TMS9900's instruction encoding, specifying register 0 in an indexed-addressing field tells the decoder to perform direct (symbolic) addressing without adding any register.

questions.prompt: What clever trick became possible if two TMS9900 routines positioned their register workspaces so they partially overlapped in RAM?
choices: The CPU doubled its clock speed by reading both blocks simultaneously
The routines shared data directly without copying arguments between registers
The hardware automatically compressed 16-bit numbers into 8-bit bytes
Both routines gained permission to run inside the Status Register
questions.explanation: Overlapping workspaces made one routine's upper registers occupy the exact same RAM addresses as another routine's lower registers, allowing zero-copy parameter passing.

chunks.title: Transistors Saved, New Superpower Unlocked
chunks.content_markdown:
Looking at the TMS9900 die reveals why TI's memory-to-memory gamble was such an engineering coup. By offloading sixteen 16-bit registers into external RAM, TI built a genuine 16-bit microprocessor with roughly 8,000 transistors—barely more than the 8-bit Z80! Those saved transistors bought a full 16-bit arithmetic path and a clean two-operand instruction set that felt spacious to minicomputer programmers.

Of course, moving registers off-chip was not just a space-saving trick. Think about what happens on a conventional CPU like the Z80 or 6809 whenever a program jumps to a subroutine or answers an urgent hardware interrupt: the processor has to painstakingly copy its on-chip registers out to RAM one by one so it doesn't clobber them.

On the TMS9900, your entire register set is *already* in RAM, anchored by a single 16-bit pointer. What happens when you simply point `WP` somewhere new?

questions.prompt: Roughly how did the TMS9900's transistor count compare to contemporary 8-bit chips after moving its registers to external RAM?
choices: It still required over ten times as many transistors as the Z80
It shrank to fewer than five hundred transistors on the entire die
It doubled the Z80's budget to roughly 16,000 transistors on silicon
It stayed around 8,000 transistors, close to the 8-bit Z80's budget
questions.explanation: Offloading R0–R15 to RAM kept the 16-bit TMS9900 around 8,000 transistors—remarkably close to the 8-bit Z80—while still supporting a full 16-bit ALU.

questions.prompt: Why does keeping all sixteen registers in RAM behind a single Workspace Pointer hint at a dramatic advantage during interrupts?
choices: Interrupts can bypass main memory completely and run inside ROM
External RAM automatically ignores writes whenever an interrupt fires
Changing WP moves the entire register set without pushing registers onto a stack
The CPU can execute sixteen different interrupts through R0–R15 at once
questions.explanation: Because the active registers are simply whatever 32-byte RAM block WP points to, updating WP gives an interrupt handler a brand-new set of sixteen registers without saving the old ones one by one.

sections.title: 3. Instant Context Switches (BLWP/RTWP) & the Coming Memory Wall
sections.summary: Walk through how RAM-resident registers turned full context switches into a single-step maneuver: BLWP reads a two-word transfer vector, flips to a fresh register workspace, and automatically saves the caller's WP, PC, and ST in R13–R15—while RTWP restores everything just as fast, powering stackless calls and 16-level hardware interrupts. Then uncover the historical twist: why keeping registers in external RAM made brilliant sense when 1976 CPUs and memory ran at matching speeds, before faster processors slammed into the memory wall.

chunks.title: The Interrupt Traffic Jam
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture a 1976 factory controller or minicomputer juggling a spinning disk drive, three keyboard terminals, and urgent temperature sensors. Dozens of times each second, an external device shouts for immediate attention via a hardware interrupt, forcing the CPU to perform a **context switch**—pausing one job cleanly so another can run.

On a conventional processor with on-chip registers, every context switch creates a brief traffic jam. Before the interrupt routine can safely touch the registers, the CPU must copy all of them onto a RAM stack one by one, then copy them all back afterward. Even the Z80's clever shadow register bank only provided a single backup set, leaving deeper interrupts back at square one.

Because the TMS9900 already kept `R0` through `R15` in RAM, Texas Instruments turned that traffic jam into a single smooth lane change.

questions.prompt: Why do conventional CPUs with on-chip registers face extra overhead during an interrupt context switch?
choices: They must save active registers to a RAM stack before reusing them
They must power down their clock generator until the interrupt ends
They must copy the entire program from ROM into external memory
They must clear every flag in the ALU before answering a device
questions.explanation: When registers live on silicon, an interrupt handler would overwrite the interrupted program's data unless the CPU first pushes those registers to a stack in RAM and pops them back afterward.

questions.prompt: What limitation did the Zilog Z80's shadow register bank face compared to the TMS9900's RAM workspaces?
choices: Shadow registers could only hold 4-bit numbers during interrupts
Shadow registers could not be restored after an interrupt finished
The Z80 provided only one extra backup set of registers on silicon
The Z80 required external clock chips to swap into its shadow bank
questions.explanation: The Z80's shadow bank gave programmers just one alternate register set on silicon, whereas the TMS9900 could define dozens of separate 32-byte workspaces anywhere in RAM.

chunks.title: Two Words and a Single Leap: BLWP and RTWP
chunks.content_markdown:
TI's instant context-switch engine hinges on two memorable instructions: **`BLWP`** (*Branch and Load Workspace Pointer*) and **`RTWP`** (*Return with Workspace Pointer*). Instead of pointing directly at code, `BLWP` points to a **transfer vector**—a tiny two-word pair in memory where the first word holds the new `WP` and the second word holds the new `PC`.

In one seamless instruction, `BLWP` switches the CPU into that brand-new register workspace and automatically preserves the caller's exact state through **workspace linkage**: it drops the caller's old `WP` into the new workspace's `R13`, the caller's return `PC` into `R14`, and the caller's old `ST` into `R15`. The routine now owns a completely clean set of registers (`R0`–`R12`) with zero stack pushing!

When the routine finishes, a single **`RTWP`** instruction copies `R15`, `R14`, and `R13` right back into `ST`, `PC`, and `WP`, snapping instantly back to the caller.

questions.prompt: What two values are stored inside a TMS9900 transfer vector used by BLWP?
choices: The caller's old accumulator value and the interrupt priority level
The new Workspace Pointer address and the new Program Counter address
The starting address of ROM and the total byte length of the routine
The lowest register index and the highest register index to preserve
questions.explanation: A transfer vector is a two-word pair in memory containing the target routine's new WP (first word) and new PC (second word).

questions.prompt: During a BLWP call, where does the TMS9900 automatically store the caller's old WP, PC, and ST for workspace linkage?
choices: Inside registers R0, R1, and R2 of the caller's original workspace
Inside three hidden backup flip-flops wired beside the clock pins
At the very top of main memory in a fixed hardware stack frame
Inside registers R13, R14, and R15 of the newly activated workspace
questions.explanation: BLWP automatically records the caller's old WP in R13, return PC in R14, and old ST in R15 of the new workspace so RTWP can restore all three in one instruction.

chunks.title: Tracing a Live Context Switch
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's watch a live `BLWP` call step by step. Suppose our main program is cruising along with `WP = >0100`, and at address `>2000` it executes `BLWP @VEC`, where `@VEC` simply labels the memory address holding our two-word transfer vector: `>0200` (new workspace) and `>4000` (subroutine code).

Instantly, the TMS9900 switches `WP` to `>0200`, writes the old `WP` (`>0100`) into the new `R13` at `>021A` (26 bytes past `>0200`), stores the next instruction address (`>2004`) into `R14` at `>021C`, saves `ST` into `R15` at `>021E`, and jumps `PC` to `>4000`. Notice that the main program's sixteen registers at `>0100`–`>011E` were never even touched!

Even better, TI wired all **16 prioritized hardware interrupts** (levels 0 through 15) to use this exact same transfer-vector table sitting at the bottom of memory (`>0000`–`>003E`), making interrupt entry and `RTWP` return astonishingly fast.

questions.prompt: In the walkthrough where BLWP switches WP from >0100 to >0200, what happens to the caller's registers stored at >0100–>011E?
choices: They are copied byte by byte into addresses >0200–>021E first
They are cleared to zero so the new routine starts cleanly
They remain completely untouched in RAM while the new workspace runs
They are locked in read-only mode until the system reboots
questions.explanation: Because BLWP simply points WP at a different 32-byte block (>0200), the caller's original register workspace at >0100 stays safely intact in RAM without copying a single byte.

questions.prompt: How did the TMS9900 handle its 16 prioritized hardware interrupt levels?
choices: Each interrupt level looked up a two-word transfer vector at the bottom of memory
Each interrupt level triggered an automatic hardware push of R0 through R15
All 16 interrupts shared one fixed workspace located inside the clock chip
Only interrupt level 0 could switch workspaces while levels 1–15 halted the CPU
questions.explanation: Hardware interrupt levels 0 through 15 each had their own two-word (WP, PC) transfer vector at addresses >0000 through >003E, performing the same instant workspace swap as BLWP.

chunks.title: Wait—Where Is the Hardware Stack?
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a surprise that trips up almost everyone coming from the Z80 or Motorola 6809: the TMS9900 has **no dedicated hardware stack pointer** at all! There is no `PUSH` or `POP` instruction built into the silicon.

For quick, everyday subroutines that don't need a whole fresh workspace, TI offered a lighter instruction called **`BL`** (*Branch and Link*). Instead of pushing the return address onto a stack, `BL` simply drops it into `R11`, and the subroutine returns by branching indirectly to the address stored inside `R11` (`B *R11`).

That's lightning fast for a single call—until Routine A calls Routine B, which overwrites `R11` and forgets how to get back to main! Likewise, if a `BLWP` routine ever called *itself* recursively (calling itself again before returning) using the same fixed transfer vector, it would clobber its own `R13`–`R15` linkage. To nest calls or write recursive code, TMS9900 programmers designated an ordinary register—by convention `R10`—as a software stack pointer.

questions.prompt: What happens if a subroutine invoked with BL calls a second subroutine with BL without saving R11 first?
choices: The CPU automatically allocates a brand-new 32-byte workspace in RAM
The hardware shifts the old return address down into register R12
The Status Register halts execution and triggers a stack-overflow trap
The second BL overwrites R11, erasing the original caller's return address
questions.explanation: Because BL always writes the return address into R11 and the TMS9900 lacks a hardware stack, a nested BL call overwrites R11 unless software explicitly saves it first.

questions.prompt: How did TMS9900 programmers support deeply nested or recursive subroutines without a built-in hardware stack pointer?
choices: By rewriting the program's transfer vectors inside read-only memory
By dedicating an ordinary workspace register like R10 as a software stack pointer
By disabling all 16 interrupt levels until every nested call returned
By splitting every recursive routine across sixteen separate interrupt levels
questions.explanation: Without a hardware stack pointer, programmers adopted a software convention—commonly reserving R10—to manage a stack in RAM for saving return addresses and local state.

chunks.title: Brilliant in 1976, Trapped by the Memory Wall
chunks.content_markdown:
History eventually judged TI's memory-to-memory gamble through a dramatic twist of timing. In 1976, a 3 MHz TMS9900 ticked once every 333 nanoseconds, while standard RAM chips responded in roughly 300 to 450 nanoseconds. Because external memory ran nearly as fast as the processor itself, keeping `R0`–`R15` in RAM barely slowed everyday math while making `BLWP`/`RTWP` context switches blazingly quick.

Within a decade, however, silicon transistors shrank and CPU clock speeds skyrocketed far faster than external DRAM access times. Computer architects call this widening gap between fast processor logic and slower off-chip memory the **memory wall**. Once on-chip registers became ten times faster than external RAM, crossing the memory bus for every single register access turned from a clever bargain into a severe speed penalty.

Yet in 1976, before that wall closed in, TI's saved silicon bought two rare minicomputer superpowers—what did TI spend those extra transistors on?

questions.prompt: Why did storing general-purpose registers in external RAM make strong engineering sense in 1976?
choices: Mid-1970s CPUs and RAM ran at comparable speeds, minimizing register-access penalties
External RAM chips in 1976 were already ten times faster than on-chip CPU logic
Software compilers in 1976 could not generate code for processors with on-chip registers
Only external RAM could retain 16-bit numbers during a four-phase clock cycle
questions.explanation: In 1976, 3 MHz CPU cycle times and standard RAM access times were closely matched, so fetching registers from external RAM carried little speed penalty while saving silicon and accelerating context switches.

questions.prompt: What does the 'memory wall' refer to in computer architecture?
choices: The physical ceramic barrier separating a CPU's address pins from its data pins
The strict 64-kilobyte addressing limit imposed by a 16-bit address bus
A hardware protection circuit that prevents programs from overwriting ROM
The growing speed gap between rapidly accelerating CPUs and slower off-chip RAM
questions.explanation: The memory wall describes how processor clock speeds climbed far faster than external memory access speeds, penalizing architectures that rely heavily on off-chip memory trips.

sections.title: 4. Minicomputer Muscle on Silicon: Hardware MPY, DIV & XOP Traps
sections.summary: See where TI spent the silicon budget saved by moving registers into RAM: genuine unsigned 16-by-16 hardware multiply (MPY) producing 32-bit results across adjacent registers, and rare 32-by-16 hardware divide (DIV) returning both quotient and remainder in one instruction with overflow checks. Then explore Extended Operations (XOP), sixteen numbered software traps that hand an operand's address to a fresh handler workspace so older or smaller chips can emulate future hardware instructions.

chunks.title: Beyond Shift-and-Add Loops
chunks.content_markdown:
If you wrote a game or payroll program on a Zilog Z80 in 1976 and needed to multiply two numbers, you hit a speed bump: the Z80 had no multiply or divide instructions at all. Programmers had to craft tedious software loops that shifted bits and added over and over. Two years later, the Motorola 6809 thrilled coders with an 8-by-8 hardware multiplier (`MUL`)—yet even the 6809 topped out at 8-bit inputs and still offered zero hardware division.

Texas Instruments played in a different weight class. By keeping `R0`–`R15` out in external RAM, TI freed enough silicon and internal microcode (the tiny step-by-step control recipes built inside a CPU) on the 1976 TMS9900 to deliver real minicomputer arithmetic right out of the box.

Not only could the TMS9900 multiply full 16-bit values in hardware—it could divide 32-bit numbers in a single instruction, a luxury almost unheard of on 1970s microchips.

questions.prompt: How did the 1976 TMS9900's built-in arithmetic capabilities compare to the Zilog Z80 and Motorola 6809?
choices: All three chips offered identical 16-bit hardware multiply and divide instructions
The TMS9900 omitted multiplication entirely in favor of faster text shifting
The 6809 included full 32-bit division while the TMS9900 handled only 8-bit math
The TMS9900 offered 16-bit multiply and 32-bit divide unmatched by 8-bit rivals
questions.explanation: The Z80 lacked both hardware multiply and divide, and the 6809 had only an 8-by-8 multiply, whereas the TMS9900 featured 16-by-16 hardware multiply and 32-by-16 hardware divide.

questions.prompt: What architectural trade-off freed enough silicon room on the 1976 TMS9900 for built-in multiply and divide logic?
choices: Eliminating the 16-bit ALU in favor of a 4-bit serial adder
Moving general-purpose registers R0–R15 off silicon into external RAM
Removing hardware interrupt support from the processor instruction set
Requiring an external math co-processor chip to run every addition
questions.explanation: Offloading sixteen 16-bit registers into RAM workspaces conserved die area, allowing TI to spend its transistor budget on a full 16-bit datapath plus microcoded MPY and DIV.

chunks.title: Pairing Registers for 32-Bit Precision
chunks.content_markdown:
Full 16-bit arithmetic immediately raises a storage problem: multiply two 16-bit unsigned numbers—say, $$50{,}000 \times 50{,}000$$—and the answer climbs past two billion, bursting far outside a single 16-bit register's $$65{,}535$$ ceiling. TI solved this cleanly with a **double-word operand**, gluing two neighboring workspace registers (`Rd` and `Rd+1`) together to hold one 32-bit number.

The unsigned multiply instruction **`MPY`** multiplies any 16-bit source value by destination register `Rd`, then stores the upper 16 bits of the 32-bit product in `Rd` and the lower 16 bits in `Rd+1`.

Even bolder was TI's genuine **hardware divider**—dedicated processor logic that performs binary long division automatically. The **`DIV`** instruction takes a 32-bit unsigned dividend spanning `Rd` and `Rd+1`, divides it by any 16-bit source divisor, and writes both the 16-bit quotient (`Rd`) and the 16-bit remainder (`Rd+1`) back in one instruction.

questions.prompt: Why does the TMS9900's MPY instruction write its answer across two consecutive workspace registers?
choices: Multiplying two 16-bit numbers can yield a 32-bit result too wide for one register
The TMS9900 splits every 16-bit answer into two 8-bit registers for backward compatibility
The first register stores the answer while the second stores a backup copy for interrupts
Each RAM workspace register can only hold positive numbers up to 255
questions.explanation: The product of two 16-bit unsigned integers can require up to 32 bits, so MPY uses a double-word operand across Rd (high 16 bits) and Rd+1 (low 16 bits).

questions.prompt: After a valid DIV instruction completes on the TMS9900, what values sit in registers Rd and Rd+1?
choices: The original divisor in Rd and the original 32-bit dividend in Rd+1
The rounded floating-point answer in Rd and the sign bit in Rd+1
The 16-bit quotient in Rd and the 16-bit remainder in Rd+1
The upper half of the quotient in Rd and the lower half in Rd+1
questions.explanation: DIV divides the 32-bit dividend in (Rd, Rd+1) by a 16-bit divisor and leaves the 16-bit integer quotient in Rd and the 16-bit remainder in Rd+1.

chunks.title: Watching MPY and DIV in Action
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's walk through a concrete round trip with numbers you can check in your head. Suppose `R1` holds $$1{,}000$$ and `R2` holds $$100$$. When the CPU executes `MPY R1, R2`, it computes $$1{,}000 \times 100 = 100{,}000$$. Since one 16-bit word wraps every $$65{,}536$$ ($$2^{16}$$), we split $$100{,}000 = 1 \times 65{,}536 + 34{,}464$$. In roughly 52 clock cycles, the TMS9900 places `1` in `R2` (the high word) and `34,464` in `R3` (the low word).

Now keep that exact 32-bit double-word `100,000` sitting in `R2` and `R3`, load `300` into `R4`, and run `DIV R4, R2`. Because $$100{,}000 = 300 \times 333 + 100$$, the hardware divider finishes in roughly 92 to 124 cycles—far faster than a multi-hundred-cycle software loop—leaving quotient `333` in `R2` and remainder `100` in `R3`.

questions.prompt: If R1 holds 1,000 and R2 holds 100, what values sit in R2 and R3 right after executing MPY R1, R2?
choices: R2 holds 100,000 and R3 holds 0
R2 holds 1 and R3 holds 34,464
R2 holds 34,464 and R3 holds 1
R2 holds 1,000 and R3 holds 100
questions.explanation: Since $$100{,}000 = 1 \times 65{,}536 + 34{,}464$$, MPY writes the upper 16-bit word (1) into the destination register R2 and the lower 16-bit word (34,464) into R3.

questions.prompt: When dividing the 32-bit value 100,000 (in R2 and R3) by 300 (in R4) using DIV R4, R2, what does R3 hold afterward?
choices: The integer quotient 333
The original divisor 300
The high word value 1
The integer remainder 100
questions.explanation: Because $$100{,}000 \div 300$$ equals 333 with a remainder of 100, DIV places the quotient (333) in R2 and the remainder (100) in R3.

chunks.title: Overflow Guardrails and the XOP Trap Door
chunks.content_markdown:
Even great hardware math has sharp edges. First, both `MPY` and `DIV` on the original TMS9900 handled only **unsigned** (non-negative) integers—if you needed negative numbers, software had to track signs manually. Second, `DIV` guarded against impossible answers: if the divisor was zero, or if the high word `Rd` was greater than or equal to the divisor, the quotient could not fit in 16 bits. In that case, the TMS9900 safely aborted the divide without corrupting `Rd` and raised the Status Register's overflow flag.

What about operations TI didn't wire into 1976 silicon, like floating-point (decimal-fraction) math or custom operating-system calls? TI added sixteen **Extended Operations (`XOP`)**—software traps numbered 0 through 15. Like `BLWP`, an `XOP` swaps workspaces through a fixed transfer-vector table (`>0040`–`>007E`), *and* automatically computes the source operand's effective memory address and drops it straight into the handler's `R11`!

questions.prompt: What happens on the TMS9900 if a DIV instruction's divisor is zero or less than or equal to the dividend's high word Rd?
choices: The CPU wraps the quotient silently and clears all Status Register flags
The processor automatically expands the quotient across three workspace registers
The CPU aborts the division, leaves the operand intact, and sets the overflow flag
The hardware switches into a built-in floating-point mode to compute a fraction
questions.explanation: If the divisor is zero or less than or equal to Rd, the quotient cannot fit in 16 bits, so DIV aborts without corrupting Rd/Rd+1 and sets the Status Register overflow bit.

questions.prompt: Beyond switching workspaces like BLWP, what extra step does an Extended Operation (XOP) automatically perform for its handler routine?
choices: It computes the source operand's effective address and places it into the handler's R11
It converts unsigned numbers into negative integers before entering the handler
It copies all sixteen caller registers directly into the handler's workspace
It pauses the four-phase clock until the external memory finishes refreshing
questions.explanation: An XOP instruction works like a BLWP trap through vectors >0040–>007E, plus it resolves the instruction's source operand address and delivers it straight into the handler's R11.

chunks.title: Software Today, Silicon Tomorrow
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and see why `XOP` was such a smart minicomputer idea. Across the TI 990 family, an application could invoke `XOP 1` to run a floating-point square root or format text. On a budget single-chip TMS9900 machine, `XOP 1` trapped cleanly into a software routine via its transfer vector; on a high-end rack-mounted TI 990 model, custom hardware could recognize and execute that exact same opcode directly in silicon! Software ran unchanged across both tiers.

Between 16-by-16 `MPY`, 32-by-16 `DIV`, and extensible `XOP` traps, TI proved that its off-chip workspace gamble paid real dividends in computational muscle.

So far, we've watched the TMS9900 move 16-bit words across memory and crunch 32-bit numbers. Yet industrial controllers and home computers also spend huge amounts of time flipping tiny single-bit switches—an indicator lamp, a motor relay, a keyboard key. Why move a whole 16-bit word just to flip one bit?

questions.prompt: Why was TI's Extended Operation (XOP) design valuable across a family of differently priced TI 990 computers?
choices: It guaranteed every TI 990 model ran at the exact same clock frequency
It let low-end chips emulate in software what high-end models could run in hardware
It prevented programmers from writing unsigned MPY or DIV instructions
It replaced the need for external RAM workspaces on entry-level boards
questions.explanation: XOP traps allowed identical machine code to run across product tiers: budget systems emulated the operation in a trap handler, while pricier systems could implement it directly in hardware.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures how the TMS9900 handled arithmetic and future instruction extensions?
choices: It omitted hardware division and relied on Z80-style prefix bytes for extensions
It restricted arithmetic to 8-bit bytes and banned software-trapped instructions
It combined unsigned hardware MPY and DIV with XOP software traps for missing operations
It built hardware decimal-fraction math onto silicon while skipping integer multiply
questions.explanation: The TMS9900 provided genuine unsigned hardware MPY and DIV on silicon and used sixteen numbered XOP traps to let software cleanly emulate missing operations like floating-point math.

sections.title: 5. One Bit at a Time: The CRU Serial I/O Paradigm
sections.summary: Contrast byte-wide I/O ports and memory-mapped peripherals with TI's distinctive Communications Register Unit (CRU), a serial bus using just three dedicated pins and workspace register R12 to reach up to 4,096 individual input and output bits. Trace single-bit commands (SBO, SBZ, TB) and variable-width serial shifts (LDCR, STCR) in action across keyboards, relays, and industrial interfaces—and weigh pin-saving elegance against bulk transfer speed.

chunks.title: Why Move Eight Bits to Flip One Switch?
chunks.content_markdown:
In the 8-bit world, CPUs talked to outside devices in one of two ways: byte-wide I/O ports (like the Z80's `IN` and `OUT` instructions) or memory-mapped I/O (like the Motorola 6809 treating hardware ports as ordinary memory addresses). Both approaches always moved a whole 8-bit byte at a time.

Imagine a factory controller—or a home computer—wired to eight unrelated switches packed into one 8-bit port: a warning lamp, a cassette motor, a printer strobe, and five keyboard lines. To turn on just the cassette motor without disturbing the other seven devices, an 8-bit CPU suffers **read-modify-write overhead**: it must read the entire byte, combine it with a bitmask to flip only one bit, and write the whole byte back.

Inherited from the TI 990 minicomputer, the TMS9900 offered a remarkably clean third option designed specifically for individual switches.

questions.prompt: What causes read-modify-write overhead when an 8-bit CPU flips a single hardware control line on a shared byte-wide port?
choices: The CPU must pause all interrupts while waiting for the power rail to settle
The CPU must read the full byte, mask one bit, and write the full byte back
The peripheral must translate every 8-bit byte into a 16-bit double-word operand
The program must copy the entire port table into external DRAM before writing
questions.explanation: When eight devices share one byte-wide port, changing a single bit safely requires reading the current byte, modifying just the target bit with a mask, and writing the byte back.

questions.prompt: How did traditional Z80 I/O ports and Motorola 6809 memory-mapped I/O resemble each other despite using different instructions?
choices: Both transferred data in full byte-wide chunks rather than addressing individual bits
Both required a dedicated 64-pin ceramic package to wire external keyboards
Both shifted every output signal serially across a single one-bit wire
Both stored hardware switch settings inside workspace register R12
questions.explanation: Although the Z80 used dedicated port instructions and the 6809 used memory addresses, both communicated with peripherals in full 8-bit bytes rather than individual hardware bits.

chunks.title: A Private Doorbell for Every Single Bit
chunks.content_markdown:
Texas Instruments called its third I/O path the **Communications Register Unit (`CRU`)**, a dedicated serial interface that gives the processor direct **bit-addressable I/O**—the ability to read or change any individual hardware line by its own bit address without touching its neighbors.

Think of byte-wide I/O like mailing a letter to an eight-unit apartment building and asking all eight tenants to pass it around. The CRU instead wires a private doorbell straight to each individual switch.

Electrically, the design was wonderfully thrifty. It needed only **three** dedicated CRU pins on the TMS9900: `CRUIN` to receive one bit, `CRUOUT` to send one bit, and `CRUCLK` to pulse an output latch. Teamed with 12 lines from the address bus, those three pins individually addressed up to $$2^{12} = 4{,}096$$ input bits and $$4{,}096$$ output bits, anchored from a base address stored inside workspace register **`R12`**.

questions.prompt: How many individual input bits and output bits could the TMS9900's CRU address using its 12 address lines and three dedicated CRU pins?
choices: Up to 64 input bits and 64 output bits
Up to 256 input bits and 256 output bits
Up to 1,024 input bits and 1,024 output bits
Up to 4,096 input bits and 4,096 output bits
questions.explanation: Using 12 address lines ($$2^{12} = 4{,}096$$) alongside separate CRUIN and CRUOUT pins, the TMS9900 could individually address 4,096 input bits and 4,096 output bits.

questions.prompt: Which workspace register did the TMS9900 reserve to hold the base address for CRU bit-addressable I/O operations?
choices: Register R0, right at the start of the active workspace
Register R10, alongside the software stack pointer
Register R12, anchoring offsets for CRU bit instructions
Register R15, shared directly with the saved Status Register
questions.explanation: By hardware design, TMS9900 CRU instructions always use workspace register R12 as the base address for locating individual peripheral bits.

chunks.title: SBO, SBZ, TB, and Shifting Multi-Bit Fields
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch how cleanly CRU code reads in practice. Suppose a system attaches a keyboard scanner and cassette recorder through TI's companion **TMS9901** programmable interface chip, and we load its CRU base address into `R12`.

Need to spin up the cassette motor wired to bit offset 6? One surgical instruction—**`SBO 6`** (*Set Bit to One*)—drives that exact pin high without disturbing any neighboring line. Ready to stop the tape? **`SBZ 6`** (*Set Bit to Zero*) drops it low. Want to check whether a key wired to bit offset 3 is pressed? **`TB 3`** (*Test Bit*) reads that single wire over `CRUIN` and places the result directly into the Status Register's Equal flag so the next line can branch immediately.

What if a peripheral needs several bits—like a 7-bit character or a 14-bit timer count? **`LDCR`** (*Load Communications Register*) shifts 1 to 16 bits serially out through `CRUOUT`, while **`STCR`** (*Store Communications Register*) shifts 1 to 16 bits back in from `CRUIN`.

questions.prompt: Which trio of TMS9900 CRU instructions handles setting, clearing, and reading a single hardware bit directly?
choices: SBO, SBZ, and TB
BLWP, RTWP, and XOP
MPY, DIV, and LDCR
BL, STCR, and WP
questions.explanation: SBO (Set Bit to One), SBZ (Set Bit to Zero), and TB (Test Bit) operate directly on a single CRU bit relative to the base address in R12.

questions.prompt: What do the CRU instructions LDCR and STCR accomplish when a peripheral needs more than a single control bit?
choices: They switch the TMS9900 into an 8-bit Z80-compatible port mode
They copy an entire 32-byte workspace directly into external ROM
They bypass the CRU pins to send parallel 16-bit bursts over RAM
They serially shift between 1 and 16 bits out to or in from CRU lines
questions.explanation: LDCR (Load Communications Register) serially outputs 1 to 16 bits over CRUOUT, while STCR (Store Communications Register) serially reads 1 to 16 bits from CRUIN.

chunks.title: Pin Thrift vs. Bulk Speed
chunks.content_markdown:
If bit-addressable CRU I/O was so crisp and pin-thrifty, why didn't it replace parallel buses everywhere? Every engineering choice carries a trade-off. Because `LDCR` and `STCR` march bits one by one across a single serial wire—pulsing `CRUCLK` for each individual bit—transferring a full 16-bit value takes dozens of clock cycles.

That made the CRU unbeatable for low-cost, low-speed control: flipping relays, scanning keyboards, reading industrial limit switches, or talking to simple chips with almost zero glue logic. Even a bare 1-bit latch chip could connect right to the CRU! Yet high-speed video graphics or fast disk drives still needed parallel memory-mapped buses that moved whole bytes or words in a single beat.

Programmers also had to watch a subtle `LDCR`/`STCR` twist: transferring 1 to 8 bits automatically accessed a single byte operand, whereas transferring 9 to 16 bits switched to a full word-aligned 16-bit operand.

questions.prompt: Why was the TMS9900's CRU bus poorly suited for streaming high-bandwidth video frames or fast disk blocks?
choices: CRU pins were hardwired to read-only mode and could never send output
Serial bit-by-bit transfers took far more clock cycles than parallel word transfers
Using CRU instructions permanently cleared all sixteen registers in the workspace
The CRU bus could only operate when the external four-phase clock was paused
questions.explanation: Because LDCR and STCR shift data one bit per pulse across a single serial wire, CRU excels at low-rate bit control but is far slower than parallel memory-mapped transfers for bulk data.

questions.prompt: How did LDCR and STCR change their operand behavior depending on the number of bits transferred?
choices: Transfers of 1–8 bits used external RAM while 9–16 bits used ROM
Transfers of 1–8 bits sent outputs while 9–16 bits always read inputs
Transfers of 1–8 bits used byte operands while 9–16 bits used word operands
Transfers of 1–8 bits skipped R12 while 9–16 bits skipped the address bus
questions.explanation: On the TMS9900, LDCR and STCR treat bit counts of 1 through 8 as byte-oriented operations and counts of 9 through 16 as 16-bit word-oriented operations.

chunks.title: A 16-Bit Dream Meets Living-Room Reality
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause and survey the remarkable 1976 chip we have assembled across these first five sections. The TMS9900 brought a full 16-bit minicomputer architecture onto single-chip silicon: a non-multiplexed 16-bit data bus, relocatable RAM register workspaces, single-instruction `BLWP`/`RTWP` context switches, genuine unsigned 16-by-16 `MPY` and 32-by-16 `DIV`, extensible `XOP` traps, and surgical CRU bit-addressable I/O.

On paper, dropping this powerhouse into a consumer home computer in 1979 should have embarrassed every 8-bit rival from Apple, Atari, and Commodore. Imagine walking into a department store and seeing a genuine 16-bit minicomputer chip sitting next to 8-bit toys!

Yet when Texas Instruments actually shipped its famous home computers, reviewers and programmers were baffled to discover that everyday programs ran noticeably *slower* than on 8-bit machines. How could engineers take such a formidable 16-bit processor and accidentally tie both of its hands behind its back?

questions.prompt: Which combination of features made the raw TMS9900 architecture look formidable on paper against 1970s 8-bit home-computer CPUs?
choices: Single-voltage 40-pin packaging, a Direct Page register, and Z80 binary compatibility
Sixteen on-chip 32-bit registers, dual hardware stacks, and built-in DRAM refresh
Zero external support chips, shadow register banks, and 8-bit prefix-byte loops
A 16-bit data bus, fast BLWP switches, hardware MPY/DIV, and CRU I/O
questions.explanation: With a true 16-bit data path, instant workspace context switching, hardware 16-by-16 multiply and 32-by-16 divide, and CRU bit I/O, the TMS9900 outclassed 8-bit CPUs on raw architectural features.

questions.prompt: What central paradox defines the transition from the TMS9900's chip architecture to Texas Instruments' home computers?
choices: TI forgot to include the TMS9900 inside its home computers and shipped a 4-bit chip instead
Despite its genuine 16-bit TMS9900 CPU, TI's home computers felt slower than 8-bit rivals
Home-computer buyers rejected the TMS9900 solely because it lacked hardware multiplication
The TMS9900 ran too fast for televisions to display any text or graphics on screen
questions.explanation: Although the TI-99/4 and TI-99/4A boasted a genuine 16-bit TMS9900 processor, surrounding system bottlenecks made everyday software feel surprisingly sluggish compared to 8-bit competitors.

sections.title: 6. The Cancelled TMS9985 & the TI-99/4's 8-Bit Chokepoint
sections.summary: Begin the cautionary tale of the TI-99/4 (1979) and TI-99/4A (1981): how TI designed its home computer around the planned 40-pin, 8-bit-bus TMS9985 with on-chip RAM, only to cancel the chip and drop the 64-pin TMS9900 onto a cost-cut 8-bit board. Follow every 16-bit word as an 8-bit bus multiplexer splits it into two slow byte cycles padded with wait states—leaving just 256 bytes of fast 16-bit scratchpad RAM as the CPU's lone express lane.

chunks.title: A Motherboard Built for a Ghost Chip
chunks.content_markdown:
When Texas Instruments unveiled the **TI-99/4** in 1979—and its sleeker, full-keyboard **TI-99/4A** successor in 1981—ads proudly celebrated the first 16-bit home computer. Yet the machine's biggest flaw began with a chip that never shipped.

TI's Consumer Products Group had *not* designed the console around the bulky 64-pin TMS9900. Their blueprint centered on the planned **TMS9985**: an economical 40-pin cousin running the same 16-bit instruction set over an inexpensive 8-bit external data bus—crucially equipped with 256 bytes of fast 16-bit RAM built right onto the CPU die so register workspaces would never clog the narrow external bus.

In late 1978, silicon troubles forced TI to cancel the TMS9985. Unwilling to delay launch and redesign the entire 8-bit motherboard, engineers bolted the full 64-pin TMS9900 straight onto a circuit board never meant to feed it.

questions.prompt: Which planned processor was the TI-99/4 motherboard originally designed to use before silicon problems forced its cancellation?
choices: The 40-pin Zilog Z80 paired with a TI emulator
The Motorola 6809 paired with a custom bus adapter
The 40-pin TMS9985 with an 8-bit bus and on-chip RAM
The multi-board discrete logic CPU from the TI 990/10
questions.explanation: TI originally engineered the home computer around the planned 40-pin, 8-bit-bus TMS9985 (which would have included 256 bytes of on-chip RAM) before cancelling it and substituting the TMS9900.

questions.prompt: Why would the planned TMS9985's 256 bytes of on-chip RAM have been so important on an 8-bit motherboard?
choices: It would have kept register workspaces fast on silicon instead of crossing the narrow 8-bit bus
It would have stored entire video games without requiring plug-in cartridges or cassette tapes
It would have eliminated the need for a keyboard or television connection on the TI-99/4
It would have converted 16-bit TI instructions automatically into 8-bit Apple II programs
questions.explanation: Because the 9900 architecture stores R0–R15 in RAM, keeping the register workspace inside fast on-chip 16-bit RAM would have shielded everyday register operations from the slower 8-bit external bus.

chunks.title: Two Lanes Crammed Through a One-Lane Tollbooth
chunks.content_markdown:
Dropping a 16-bit TMS9900 onto an 8-bit board created an immediate plumbing crisis. Wiring full 16-bit memory across the entire console and its expansion ports would have doubled memory chip counts and blown the retail price budget. Instead, TI put a **bus multiplexer** between the CPU and almost the entire system.

A **bus multiplexer** is a switching circuit that funnels a wide data path through a narrower one in multiple steps—like forcing a wide two-lane freight train to split its cargo through a single-lane tollbooth. Whenever the TMS9900 asked for a 16-bit word across the 8-bit bus, the multiplexer fetched the high byte first, latched it temporarily, fetched the low byte second, and finally handed the reassembled 16-bit word to the processor.

While that two-step shuffle dragged on, the motherboard asserted **wait states**—forced pause cycles that froze the TMS9900 in place until the slower 8-bit bus finished delivering both halves.

questions.prompt: What job did the 8-bit bus multiplexer perform inside the TI-99/4 and TI-99/4A?
choices: It doubled the TMS9900's clock speed by merging two four-phase clocks together
It translated CRU serial bits directly into television color signals
It allowed two TMS9900 chips to share a single 64-pin ceramic socket
It split every 16-bit CPU memory transfer into two sequential 8-bit byte transfers
questions.explanation: The bus multiplexer bridged the TMS9900's 16-bit data pins to the console's cheaper 8-bit bus by breaking every 16-bit word access into two consecutive 8-bit transfers.

questions.prompt: In microprocessor hardware, what is a wait state?
choices: A software loop programmers write to pause a video game between levels
An extra idle clock cycle inserted to hold the CPU until slower memory responds
A low-power sleep mode that turns off the external power rails overnight
A backup register workspace reserved exclusively for level-15 interrupts
questions.explanation: Wait states are hardware-enforced pause cycles that temporarily stall the CPU clock sequence so slower buses or memory chips have time to finish a transfer.

chunks.title: Compounding the Wait-State Tax
chunks.content_markdown:
Now put two pieces of the puzzle together and watch the performance hit explode. On the TI-99/4 and 99/4A, every single 16-bit access crossing the 8-bit bus multiplexer incurred **four wait states** on top of the normal bus timing.

On a conventional CPU with on-chip registers, a wait-state bus mainly slows down fetching instructions and loading occasional variables. Remember, though, that the TMS9900's memory-to-memory architecture stores all sixteen registers `R0`–`R15` in RAM! If a program places its register workspace out in 8-bit expansion memory, even an ordinary register addition like `A R1, R4` triggers *four* separate 8-bit-multiplexed round trips: fetching the instruction, reading `R1`, reading `R4`, and writing `R4` back.

Worse still, the TMS9900's internal bus logic often performed a read-before-write even on full word stores, adding yet another slow trip through the 8-bit tollbooth!

questions.prompt: Why did the TI-99/4A's 4-wait-state 8-bit bus hurt the TMS9900 far more severely than it would hurt a conventional CPU with on-chip registers?
choices: The TMS9900 had to reboot its four-phase clock after every wait state
Wait states disabled the TMS9900's hardware multiply and divide circuits
With R0–R15 in RAM, every register access paid the wait-state penalty
The bus multiplexer forced all 16-bit numbers to be recalculated as 8-bit sums
questions.explanation: In a memory-to-memory CPU, ordinary register reads and writes are memory accesses—so placing a workspace behind the 4-wait-state 8-bit multiplexer slowed down every single register operation.

questions.prompt: In the example A R1, R4 with both code and workspace sitting in 8-bit expansion RAM, why do wait states pile up so rapidly?
choices: Instruction fetch, reading R1 and R4, and writing R4 all cross the 8-bit bus
The CPU must read all sixteen registers R0 through R15 before adding any two of them
The 8-bit multiplexer converts every addition into sixteen separate CRU serial pulses
Each register value must be copied through ROM twice before entering the ALU
questions.explanation: With code and workspace on the 8-bit bus, instruction fetch, both source/destination register reads, and the final writeback all suffer 8-bit multiplexing and 4-wait-state delays.

chunks.title: A 256-Byte Express Lane: Fast Scratchpad RAM
chunks.content_markdown:
Mercifully, not *every* wire on the TI-99/4A motherboard passed through that sluggish 8-bit funnel. To stand in for the 256 bytes of on-chip RAM lost when the TMS9985 died, TI wired two tiny islands directly onto the TMS9900's true 16-bit bus with **zero wait states**: the console's 8 KB system ROM (`>0000`–`>1FFF`) and a tiny **256 bytes of fast 16-bit scratchpad RAM** (`>8300`–`>83FF`).

**Scratchpad RAM** is a small patch of high-speed, directly connected memory meant for the CPU's hottest working data. On the TI-99/4A, those 256 bytes were pure gold. Because one TMS9900 register workspace needs only 32 bytes, putting your workspace inside `>8300`–`>83FF` let `R0`–`R15` run at full native 16-bit, zero-wait-state speed—bypassing the 8-bit multiplexer completely!

Still, 256 bytes is tiny—barely enough for a few workspaces, system pointers, and a handful of critical variables.

questions.prompt: How much fast, zero-wait-state 16-bit scratchpad RAM did TI wire directly onto the TI-99/4A's 16-bit CPU bus?
choices: 32 bytes, enough for exactly one workspace
256 bytes, standing in for the cancelled TMS9985's on-chip RAM
16 kilobytes, holding all user programs at full 16-bit speed
64 kilobytes, covering the entire TMS9900 address space
questions.explanation: TI wired just 256 bytes of zero-wait-state 16-bit scratchpad RAM (at >8300–>83FF) directly to the 16-bit bus as an external substitute for the cancelled TMS9985's on-chip RAM.

questions.prompt: What immediate advantage did a program gain by placing its 32-byte register workspace inside the TI-99/4A's scratchpad RAM?
choices: It doubled the size of every register from 16 to 32 bits
It doubled the width of the CRU serial peripheral output pins
It let hardware interrupts run without needing two-word transfer vectors
Every register read and write bypassed the wait-state 8-bit multiplexer
questions.explanation: Because scratchpad RAM sat directly on the un-multiplexed 16-bit bus with zero wait states, placing a register workspace there restored full-speed native register accesses.

chunks.title: Wait—Where Did the Other 16 Kilobytes Go?
chunks.content_markdown:
Take a breath and review the first layer of TI's cautionary tale. A single cancelled chip—the 40-pin TMS9985—pushed Texas Instruments into squeezing a full 64-pin TMS9900 behind an 8-bit bus multiplexer that sliced every 16-bit transfer in two and padded it with four wait states. Only the 8 KB console ROM and 256 bytes of fast 16-bit scratchpad RAM escaped the chokepoint.

Yet if you picked up a TI-99/4A box at Sears or Toys 'R' Us in 1981, bold letters on the front promised **'16K RAM'** right out of the box—matching the Atari 400 and dwarfing the Commodore VIC-20's 5 KB!

Wait a second: if the TMS9900 only had 256 bytes of RAM wired to its own CPU bus, where on earth were those 16,384 bytes of advertised user memory sitting? The answer leads straight to one of the most ingenious—and most awkwardly wired—chips inside the console.

questions.prompt: Which two memory regions inside an unexpanded TI-99/4A sat directly on the TMS9900's un-multiplexed 16-bit bus?
choices: The 8 KB console ROM and the 256-byte fast scratchpad RAM
The 16 KB of advertised user DRAM and the plug-in cartridge slot
The cassette tape buffer and the external printer expansion port
The entire 64 KB address map except for the bottom 256 bytes
questions.explanation: Only the 8 KB console ROM (>0000–>1FFF) and the 256 bytes of scratchpad RAM (>8300–>83FF) connected directly to the 16-bit zero-wait-state bus.

questions.prompt: What puzzle arises when comparing the TI-99/4A's advertised '16K RAM' with the CPU's direct 256-byte scratchpad RAM?
choices: The box misprinted 256 bytes as 16 kilobytes due to a hexadecimal typo
The remaining 16 KB sat inside read-only cartridges that users could not edit
The console's 16 KB user RAM was not wired to the CPU bus
The TMS9900's 15-bit address bus was incapable of addressing more than 256 bytes
questions.explanation: Although the TI-99/4A contained 16 KB of dynamic RAM, that memory was not directly wired to the TMS9900's address bus—it lived behind another specialized chip inside the console.

sections.title: 7. Sixteen Kilobytes Behind Glass: The TMS9918A VDP Bottleneck
sections.summary: Meet the TMS9918 and TMS9918A Video Display Processor—a standout graphics chip with colorful tile screens and 32 hardware sprites that went on to power classics like the MSX and ColecoVision—and see how TI's penny-pinching turned it into a memory bottleneck. Discover why the TI-99/4A's advertised 16 KB of user RAM was wired exclusively behind the VDP instead of the CPU bus, forcing the TMS9900 to shuttle program bytes one at a time through indirect video ports.

chunks.title: A Star Graphics Chip Given an Impossible Side Job
chunks.content_markdown:
Open a TI-99/4A and you will spot a chip that genuinely deserved every ounce of praise it received: the **TMS9918A** (upgraded from the 1979 TI-99/4's TMS9918). Designed right inside Texas Instruments, it was so capable and affordable that rival companies later snapped it up to power the ColecoVision console, Sega's SG-1000, and the entire MSX home-computer family.

Yet inside TI's own home computer, bean-counters handed this stellar graphics chip an awkward second job. Rather than pay for a separate 16-kilobyte bank of dynamic RAM attached directly to the TMS9900 processor, TI wired the console's **entire 16 KB of user RAM** exclusively to the video chip!

That single cost-cutting shortcut saved a handful of dollars per console—and trapped the TMS9900 behind an invisible wall of glass.

questions.prompt: Why did Texas Instruments wire the TI-99/4A's 16 KB of dynamic RAM exclusively to the TMS9918A video chip rather than directly to the CPU?
choices: To cut manufacturing costs by avoiding a second bank of RAM on the CPU bus
Because the TMS9900 lacked enough address pins to reach 16 kilobytes
Because dynamic RAM could not store 16-bit numbers without a video signal
To prevent third-party keyboards from reading memory through CRU ports
questions.explanation: To save component and board costs, TI avoided giving the TMS9900 its own 16 KB bank of CPU DRAM and forced the system to share the 16 KB attached to the TMS9918A video chip.

questions.prompt: What later hardware adoption demonstrated that the TMS9918A itself was a highly respected graphics chip despite the TI-99/4A's memory issues?
choices: IBM selected the TMS9918A as the main processor inside its PCs
Motorola licensed the TMS9918A to expand the 6809's Direct Page RAM
Zilog adopted the TMS9918A to replace the Z80's DRAM refresh counter
Systems like the ColecoVision, Sega SG-1000, and MSX built graphics around it
questions.explanation: The TMS9918A became an industry favorite outside TI, driving vibrant graphics in the ColecoVision, Sega SG-1000, and the MSX standard—where those machines also gave their CPUs direct main RAM.

chunks.title: Sprites, Tiles, and the Vault Receptionist
chunks.content_markdown:
The TMS9918A was a self-contained **Video Display Processor (`VDP`)**—a specialized co-processor that handled television scan timing, built-in DRAM refresh, 15 vivid colors, grid-based tile backgrounds, and full bitmap graphics on the 99/4A. Best of all, it supported up to 32 **hardware sprites**: independent movable graphic shapes drawn cleanly over the background by video silicon without forcing the CPU to erase and redraw background pixels.

The trouble was **indirect video RAM**—memory owned privately by the VDP that does not appear on the CPU's own address bus.

Picture storing all your company's filing cabinets inside a locked glass vault tended by a busy receptionist. You cannot walk in and grab a folder yourself; you have to step up to a tiny mail slot, hand over a slip with the exact drawer number, and ask the receptionist to pass you one page at a time. That was how the TMS9900 had to touch its own 16 KB of user RAM!

questions.prompt: What key visual advantage did the TMS9918A's 32 hardware sprites give game developers?
choices: They expanded the CPU's direct scratchpad memory from 256 bytes to 32 kilobytes
Video silicon drew independent movable objects over backgrounds without manual erasing
They converted monochrome vector lines automatically into 3D wireframe shapes
They allowed the CPU to execute 32 separate BASIC programs at the same time
questions.explanation: Hardware sprites let the VDP overlay up to 32 independently positioned shapes on top of the background automatically, sparing the CPU from constantly erasing and redrawing scenery.

questions.prompt: What made the TI-99/4A's 16 KB of RAM 'indirect video RAM' from the TMS9900's point of view?
choices: It could only store monochrome screen characters and refused numeric values
It vanished completely whenever the television was switched off
It sat behind the VDP and used narrow I/O port transfers
It connected directly to the CPU's 16-bit bus but ran in reverse byte order
questions.explanation: Indirect video RAM is wired privately to the VDP's own memory bus rather than the CPU's address bus, forcing the processor to read and write bytes indirectly through VDP ports.

chunks.title: Passing Every Byte Through a One-Byte Slot
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch what the TMS9900 actually had to do just to read a single byte sitting at 14-bit address `>1234` inside the TI-99/4A's 16 KB VDP RAM (since $$2^{14} = 16{,}384$$ bytes). Normally, a processor puts an address on its address pins and pulls back a full 16-bit word in one shot.

Not here! Because the VDP sat behind the console's slow 8-bit bus as a pair of memory-mapped ports, the TMS9900 had to execute a multi-step ritual: first, write the low address byte (`>34`) to the VDP address port (`>8C02`); second, write the high address byte (`>12`, plus a read/write mode bit) to `>8C02`; third, read the resulting single byte from the VDP data port (`>8800`)—or write a byte to `>8C00`.

Mercifully, the VDP automatically bumped its internal address pointer up by one after each byte, helping sequential bulk copies. Every random variable lookup, however, meant re-sending a brand-new two-byte address all over again!

questions.prompt: To read a single byte from a new random address inside the TI-99/4A's VDP RAM, what sequence did the TMS9900 have to follow?
choices: Place the 14-bit address on its address bus and fetch a full 16-bit word directly
Shift the 14-bit address serially across the CRU pins using LDCR and STCR
Copy the entire 16 KB video bank into the 256-byte scratchpad RAM first
Write both address bytes to the VDP port, then read the data port
questions.explanation: Accessing a random VDP RAM byte required writing the low and high bytes of the target address to the VDP address port (>8C02) before reading or writing one byte via the VDP data port.

questions.prompt: What built-in VDP convenience made copying a contiguous block of bytes much faster than jumping between random VDP addresses?
choices: The VDP widened its port to 16 bits automatically during block copies
The VDP auto-incremented its internal address pointer after each byte read or write
The VDP temporarily handed its 16 KB DRAM pins straight to the TMS9900
The VDP skipped screen drawing whenever the CPU started a memory transfer
questions.explanation: After each read or write through its data port, the TMS9918A automatically incremented its internal address pointer by one, letting sequential streams avoid resending two-byte addresses.

chunks.title: Dropped Bytes and Code That Could Not Run
chunks.content_markdown:
Trapping user memory behind a graphics chip triggered two startling side effects. First came strict timing contention: while painting active picture lines onto a television, the TMS9918A stayed furiously busy reading its own DRAM to fetch pixels and refresh memory rows. If fast native CPU code pushed consecutive bytes to the VDP port without inserting a tiny pause—just a few microseconds (millionths of a second)—the VDP simply missed the request and silently dropped the byte!

The second consequence was even bigger. A processor's Program Counter (`PC`) can only fetch native machine instructions from memory wired directly to the CPU's own address bus. Because the 16 KB of VDP RAM was completely invisible to the TMS9900's `PC`, an unexpanded TI-99/4A **could not execute native TMS9900 machine code from its 16 KB of built-in RAM**!
